items.text: Alcohols are an important class of organic compounds. In this chapter we will study some of their reactions.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that alcohols contain the functional group -OH

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how to draw structural and displayed formulae for methanol, ethanol, propanol (propan-1-ol only) and butanol (butan-1-ol only), and name each compound

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that ethanol can be oxidised by:

items.label: list_item
items.text: burning in air or oxygen (complete combustion)

items.label: list_item
items.text: reaction with oxygen in the air to form ethanoic acid (microbial oxidation)

items.label: list_item
items.text: heating with potassium dichromate(Vl) in dilute sulfuric acid to form ethanoic acid

items.label: text
items.text: What we commonly refer to as alcohol' is just one member of a large family (homologous series) of similar compounds. Alcohols all contain the functional group -OH covalently bonded to a carbon chain.

items.label: text
items.text: The familiar alcohol in drinks is C2H5OH (or, better, showing the structure, CH3CH2OH) and should properly be called ethanol.

items.label: list_item
items.text: reacting ethene with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst at a temperature of about 300 °C and a pressure of about 60–70 atm

items.label: list_item
items.text: the fermentation of glucose, in the absence of air, at an optimum temperature of about 30 °C and using the enzymes in yeast

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand the reasons for fermentation in the absence of air and at an optimum temperature
